name: Nikhil Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a wheel loader at Redgum, the big bauxite mine on the coast road. I'm on the stockpile, which means I load the ore that comes out of the pit into the hopper that feeds the train. It's a lot of back and forth, watching the levels, keeping the rail crew happy so the train leaves on time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady and I'm good with machines. I use AI every day, for checking the train schedule, planning my weekend jobs, even working out my fuel costs. What wears me out is the twelve-hour days and the money. I bought a second-hand skid steer last year to do weekend earthmoving jobs, levelling house blocks and driveways, and the loan means I've only got about two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful even if the big promises didn't happen. I use them every day and they save me time. I'd tell my friends at the temple not to write it off just because it wasn't magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry isn't AI. Every spare dollar I had went into a second-hand skid steer, so I'm broke on paper but I own a machine nobody can lay off. If the skid steer breaks, or the weekend work dries up, I'm in trouble, because the loan doesn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader job at Redgum and push the weekend business harder, maybe three jobs a month instead of two. I'd use AI to write quotes and find customers on the local buy-and-sell pages. And I'd pay the loan down faster so I'm not stuck if something breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. A bit stretched, but proud of what I'm building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your parents feel about the skid steer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father loves it. He ran a small shop for twenty years and says owning something is the only real security. My mother thinks I should be saving for a wedding instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A blown hydraulic hose and no weekend jobs. That's maybe a thousand gone and the loan still due. I'd have to borrow from my father, which I hate doing.

say: I'd say the tools are **still useful** even if big promises failed.
I'd tell friends at the **temple** not to write AI off.
think: My **skid steer loan** is the real risk, not AI.
A breakdown or **slow weekend** month would leave me in trouble.
do: Push the weekend business to **three jobs a month**.
S0.quote: Every spare dollar I had went into a second-hand skid steer, so I'm broke on paper but I own a machine nobody can lay off.
fieldNote: Nikhil's thin savings come from **investing** in a skid steer, not overspending.
His father's **shopkeeper** view of ownership shapes his plans.
He uses AI daily for **quotes** and finding customers.

steps.text: Keep loading the Redgum stockpile on the same roster
Book three weekend earthmoving jobs a month
Use AI to write quotes and find local customers
Pay extra off the skid steer loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a disaster, for people willing to work. I'd say the government should keep rules simple so small operators can use the new tools too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office jobs at Redgum shrink first, and the loader goes later. When robots come to the mine slowly, the smart move is to be the local guy who knows how to run them for the small jobs the big companies ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Redgum to put me on any automation trial so I learn the systems early. I'd look at a GPS guidance kit for the skid steer, so I can level house blocks faster and charge more. And I'd keep the loader job as long as it lasts, because steady pay matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. Nervous about the loan, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A GPS kit costs money. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably another small loan, which my mother would hate. I'd only do it if I had a few jobs lined up first. I'm not reckless, just impatient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Redgum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older loader drivers, like Uncle Raj, who isn't really my uncle but everyone calls him that. He's great with machines but hates screens. I'd offer to show him the AI stuff on his lunch break.

say: I'd say this is **a chance** for people willing to work.
I'd want **simple rules** so small operators can use new tools.
think: Redgum's **office jobs** shrink first and my loader later.
Small jobs the big firms ignore are **my opening**.
do: Buy a **GPS guidance kit** for the skid steer once jobs are lined up.
Keep the **loader job** for steady pay.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with some nerves about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, but people who move quickly will be fine. I'd tell everyone to start something of their own now, because waiting for the government is a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a squeeze. With AGI in 2028, my skid steer loan still has three years to run, and so does my loader job, which is a strange kind of race. By 2031 robots can drive both the loader and maybe even level a house block.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader job and save every dollar from it while it lasts. I'd use AGI tools to run the business side, quotes, bookings, accounts, so it costs me nothing in time. And I'd look at buying a second machine with a partner, so we're a real small business before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your weekend business when robots can level a block?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big companies will buy those robots first. Small jobs in town will still want someone they know for a few years. I'd want to be that person, and maybe own a robot myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say get married first, then take risks. She's probably right. But I'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone who's serious. I'd say young guys should learn a machine and start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is good for me. Five years is enough to turn my weekend jobs into a real business, if I stop being scared of the bank manager. The thinking side goes in 2031, so the paperwork's free by then, and the robots come in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader job for three years and build the business on weekends. I'd talk to the bank about a small business loan by year two. And I'd look at an AI-driven site survey drone, so I can quote jobs faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit nervous about the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you scared of the bank manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father never trusted banks. He saved cash in a tin. I know that's old-fashioned, but it's in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would marriage fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably in year two or three, if my parents' introductions work out. I'd want the business steady first. My mother would say the opposite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so nobody has an excuse to sit still. I'd say families should plan together and young people should get a trade or a machine of their own. At the temple I'd tell the parents to stop pushing every kid into an office, because the offices go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm happy with this one. My father came to this country with one suitcase, and I've got ten years' warning and a machine, so I've got no excuse to fail. The paperwork side goes to AI by 2036, which helps my business, and the robots come for hands-on work around 2039, when I'm 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader job at Redgum for four or five years and build the business on weekends. I'd pay off the skid steer, then buy machines one at a time, maybe a small excavator next. Around 2036 I'd buy a robot-ready machine myself, so I'm the one renting it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Money's still tight, but I can see the road ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad injury, or the bauxite price crashing and Redgum cutting shifts. Either one would hit me hard with two weeks of savings. That's why the loan comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, young guys from the temple, maybe two by the time I'm 35. I'd want to give them a start the way nobody gave my father one. I'd pay them properly and teach them the machines and the AI side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My loan and my job would both run out about the same time. What would help is simple rules and small business loans for people like me, so we can buy the new machines instead of being replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my kids, and I don't have any yet. I don't want the government to save me, I want it to get out of the way while I build something my kids can work in.

headlineQuote: I don't want the government to save me, I want it to get out of the way while I build something my kids can work in.
portrait: Nikhil, 27, drives a **wheel loader** on the stockpile at Redgum bauxite mine.
He put his savings into a **skid steer** for weekend earthmoving, leaving two weeks saved.
He uses AI daily and sees change as a **business chance**.
He's uneasy in most pictures and **anxious** when AGI comes in two years.
His father's **migration story** drives his self-reliance.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, when his **loan and loader job** both run out together.
whatWouldHelp: **Simple rules** and small business loans to buy new machines.
